say: You give it the chance of success on one trial, $p$, and the trial number, $n$. It finds the probability that the first success comes on trial $n$ and not before.
The key idea: trials $1$ to $n-1$ must all fail, then trial $n$ must succeed. The trials are independent, so multiply: $(1-p)^{n-1}\,p$.

how.higher: Higher level used it once, in 2022 on Paper 2 (Q10 (b), 5 marks): three fails in a row, then a success.
how.ordinary: Ordinary level used it once, in 2021 on Paper 2 (Q2 (a)(ii), 10 marks): fail, fail, then success.

example.question: A spinner lands on red with probability $\frac{1}{5}$ on each spin. Find the probability that the first red comes on the 4th spin.

steps.title: Find the two chances
steps.say: The first red is on spin 4, so spins 1, 2 and 3 are **not** red. Find the chance of a fail, $\hl{1}{q}$, and of a success, $\hl{2}{p}$.

lines.text: A fail is $\hl{1}{\frac{4}{5}}$. A success is $\hl{2}{\frac{1}{5}}$.

steps.title: Multiply the four spins
steps.say: The spins are independent, so multiply: three fails, then one success.

steps.title: Work it out
steps.say: Cube the top and the bottom of the first fraction, then multiply across.

lines.text: Write the product before you calculate it. That line earns marks on its own.

higher.tip: Write the full formula with every number put in. Fully substituted work earns high partial credit even if you slip on the arithmetic.
Keep the fail and success chances the right way round. Swapping $0.05$ and $0.95$ loses marks.

ordinary.tip: Write the failure chance as $1 - p$. That line is marked.
Writing fail, fail, success earns work of merit, so list the trials before you multiply.
If you set up the product but do not work it out, you still get high partial credit.

say: You give it the chance that both events happen, $P(A \cap B)$, and the chance of the event you are **told** has happened, $P(B)$. It finds $P(A \mid B)$.
The key idea: knowing $B$ happened shrinks the world to $B$ alone. Divide the overlap by $P(B)$. Note $P(A \mid B)$ is not the same as $P(B \mid A)$.

how.higher: Higher level uses it in 2015, 2017, 2020, 2023, 2024 and 2025, always on Paper 2 as the main skill, for 5 to 15 marks. It is usually the last step after a tree diagram or table is filled in.

example.question: In a survey, $60\%$ of people own a bike. $24\%$ own a bike and a car. A person who owns a bike is chosen at random. Find the probability that this person owns a car.

steps.title: Name the events
steps.say: Let $B$ be owning a bike and $C$ be owning a car. We are **told** the person owns a bike, so the bike is the condition.

lines.text: We want $P(C \mid B)$, the chance of a car given a bike.

steps.title: Write the rule
steps.say: The overlap goes on top. The thing we are told, $\hl{2}{P(B)}$, goes on the bottom.

lines.text: This is not $P(B \mid C)$. That would divide by $P(C)$.

steps.title: Substitute and divide
steps.say: Put in the two numbers and divide.

higher.tip: Write the formula for $P(A \mid B)$ with the numbers put in. A fully substituted formula earns high partial credit.
Find the top line and the bottom line separately. Each one that is correct earns credit.
Draw the tree diagram and fill in the branches. A tree with some correct values earns credit before you reach the answer.

say: You give it some groups of people or things, and a condition on how many to take from each. It finds the number of selections that meet the condition.
The key idea: split the condition into one choice per group, count each with ${}^nC_r$, then **multiply**.

how.higher: Higher level used it in 2019 on Paper 2 (Q1 (b), 5 marks) and in 2023 on Paper 2 (Q10 (b)(iii), 10 marks, a code with listed cases).

example.question: A committee of 4 is chosen from 6 men and 5 women. It must contain exactly 2 women. How many different committees are possible?

steps.title: Split by group
steps.say: Exactly 2 women means the other 2 members must be men. So make two separate choices: 2 from the 5 women, and 2 from the 6 men.

steps.title: Count each choice
steps.say: Order does not matter, so use ${}^nC_r$ for each group.

steps.title: Multiply the choices
steps.say: Every way of choosing the women can go with every way of choosing the men. Multiply.

higher.tip: List the cases when you can. Listing some correct codes earns work of merit.

sources.quote: Work of merit, for example, lists

higher.tip: Find the combinations first, then multiply by the number of ways to arrange each. Showing both ideas earns high partial credit.

say: You give it the number of trials $n$, the number of successes $k$, and the chance of success $p$. It finds the probability of exactly $k$ successes.
The key idea: each way of getting $k$ successes has chance $p^k(1-p)^{n-k}$, and ${}^nC_k$ counts the ways. For "at least", find the opposite and take it from $1$.

how.higher: Higher level uses it in 2020, 2021, 2022, 2024 and 2025, always on Paper 2 as the main skill, for 5 to 15 marks. 2021 used it six times. Many parts ask for "at most" or "at least" and a calculator sum.

example.question: Each bolt a machine makes is faulty with probability $0.1$, independently of the others. A box holds 8 bolts. Find the probability that at least 2 bolts in the box are faulty.

steps.title: Turn it round
steps.say: "At least 2" has many cases. The opposite, 0 or 1 faulty, has only two. So find those and take them from $1$.

steps.title: Find P(0)
steps.say: No faulty bolts: all 8 are good, each with chance $0.9$.

steps.title: Find P(1)
steps.say: One faulty bolt: 8 places it could be, one bad at $0.1$, seven good at $0.9$.

steps.title: Take them from 1
steps.say: Subtract both from $1$ and round to 4 decimal places.

higher.tip: Multiply the terms together. Writing the pieces without multiplying them does not earn the higher marks.
Get at least one whole term right: the coefficient, the power of $p$ and the power of $1-p$. A fully correct term earns mid partial credit.
For "at most" or "at least", show how you will build the answer from the terms. Saying how to find it earns credit.
Do not round early. Round the final answer, and lose a mark if you do not.
